As a result of cell signals, platelets in the area of injury aggre-
gate and stick to one another. Another protein, the von Wil-
lebrand factor, is responsible for the increased stickiness of the 
platelets. Th e inﬂ ammatory signals also act on red marrow to
increase thrombopoietin, which regulates platelet production.
Activation of protein factors results in conversion of prothrom-
bin to thrombin and ﬁ brinogen to ﬁ brin. Th e platelets and
other blood components are trapped in strands of ﬁ brin and 
form a clot. Vitamin K (essential for Factors IX, X, VII) and cal-
cium (essential for factor IV) are directly involved in clotting.27
Th e coagulation proteins (Factors IX, X, VII) that are vitamin
K-dependent are synthesized in the liver, and the receptors for 
these proteins are calcium-dependent. Compounds like the
drug warfarin, which act as anticoagulants or anticlotting com-
pounds, inhibit the ability of vitamin K and calcium to activate
the clotting proteins. Treatment with vitamin K antagonists 
like warfarin must involve patient counseling on steady-state
consumption of vitamin K-containing foods and supplements.28
